Abstract
Here is a brief summary of why this paper is important and what are the main conclusions.

Introduction

As people age, memory loss can make everyday tasks harder, so it is important to understand whether memory training provides lasting benefits. One study found that older people who received training over six years had better long-term everyday memory outcomes than those who received short-term intensive training (requena2016six?). However, additional training does not always produce noticeable benefits. In another study, improvements in some memory tasks following strategy-based memory training lasted up to eleven months, but booster sessions did not clearly improve the maintenance of those gains (borella2023effects?). These findings suggest that both the duration of training benefits and the value of additional sessions deserve attention.

The ACTIVE study provides an opportunity to examine these questions over a longer period. It randomly assigned older adults to memory training, reasoning training, speed-of-processing training, or a no-contact control group and followed their cognitive performance over ten years. Some participants were also selected for booster training at 11 and 35 months after initial training (Rebok et al. 2014). So our research question is, how do memory scores change over ten years in the memory training and control groups, and is booster training associated with smaller long-term declines in memory scores within the memory training group, after accounting for baseline age? This could help us understand whether the benefits of memory training persist as participants age and whether booster training helps maintain those benefits.

Methods

Describe and justify the statistical methods used in enough detail that the analysis could be replicated, citing original authors for methods and R packages used. Cite statistical methods such as the EM Algorithm (dempster_maximum_1977?).

Describe model selection process and criteria used to evaluate models.

We first plotted average memory scores over time for the memory training and control groups. The scores did not appear to change at a constant rate, so we treated follow-up year as a categorical variable. To decide how to include baseline age, we plotted baseline memory scores against baseline age and compared a linear regression line with a LOESS curve. The two fitting lines were similar across most of the age range, so we included baseline age as a linear term. We therefore used generalized estimating equations (GEE) because our main goal was to compare how average memory scores changed over time in the memory training and control groups. GEE allowed us to estimate these group-level changes while accounting for the correlation between repeated scores from the same participant.

Conclusions

Connect and hypothesize about results in larger context.

Talk about what you learn about the topic from your results.

One limitation is that the booster variable indicates whether participants were invited to booster training, but does not tell us whether they actually attended. Therefore, the invited group in our analysis may include participants who did not attend. We cannot draw a conclusion about whether attending the booster sessions helped participants maintain their memory scores.

## Introduction

As people age, memory loss can make everyday tasks harder, so it is important to understand whether memory training provides lasting benefits. One study found that older people who received training over six years had better long-term everyday memory outcomes than those who received short-term intensive training [@requena2016six]. However, additional training does not always produce noticeable benefits. In another study, improvements in some memory tasks following strategy-based memory training lasted up to eleven months, but booster sessions did not clearly improve the maintenance of those gains [@borella2023effects]. These findings suggest that both the duration of training benefits and the value of additional sessions deserve attention.

The ACTIVE study provides an opportunity to examine these questions over a longer period. It randomly assigned older adults to memory training, reasoning training, speed-of-processing training, or a no-contact control group and followed their cognitive performance over ten years. Some participants were also selected for booster training at 11 and 35 months after initial training [@rebok2014ten]. So our research question is, how do memory scores change over ten years in the memory training and control groups, and is booster training associated with smaller long-term declines in memory scores within the memory training group, after accounting for baseline age? This could help us understand whether the benefits of memory training persist as participants age and whether booster training helps maintain those benefits.

## Data

Describe the data source and the data itself.

Describe the variables of interest and how they were measured.
```{r results = "hide"}
#read in data
#clean data, as needed
source("cleaning_active.R")
library(tidyverse)
library(tidyr)
library(geeM)

memory_data <- activeLong %>%
  filter(INTGRP %in% c("Memory Training", "Control")) %>%
  droplevels() %>%
  mutate(INTGRP = relevel(INTGRP, ref = "Control")) %>%
  drop_na(Memory, Years, INTGRP, AgeAtBaseline) %>%
  arrange(AID, Years)

booster_data <- memory_data %>%
  filter(INTGRP == "Memory Training") %>%
  droplevels() %>%
  mutate(BOOSTER = factor(BOOSTER)) %>%
  drop_na(BOOSTER)

gee_mod1 <- memory_data %>%
  geem(Memory ~ factor(Years) * INTGRP + AgeAtBaseline, data = ., id = AID, corstr = "independence") 

gee_mod2 <- memory_data %>%
  geem(Memory ~ factor(Years) * INTGRP + AgeAtBaseline, data = ., id = AID, corstr = "exchangeable")

gee_booster <- booster_data %>%
  geem(Memory ~ factor(Years) * BOOSTER + AgeAtBaseline, data = ., id = AID, corstr = "exchangeable")

summary(gee_mod1)
summary(gee_mod2)
summary(gee_booster)
```

```{r}
memory_data %>%
  group_by(INTGRP, Years) %>%
  summarize(AverageMemory = mean(Memory, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Years, y = AverageMemory, color = INTGRP)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Average Memory Scores Over Time",
    x = "Follow Up Years",
    y = "Average Memory Score",
    color = "Treatment Group"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```


## Methods

Describe and justify the statistical methods used in enough detail that the analysis could be replicated, citing original authors for methods and R packages used. Cite statistical methods such as the EM Algorithm [@dempster_maximum_1977].

Describe model selection process and criteria used to evaluate models.

We first plotted average memory scores over time for the memory training and control groups. The scores did not appear to change at a constant rate, so we treated follow-up year as a categorical variable. To decide how to include baseline age, we plotted baseline memory scores against baseline age and compared a linear regression line with a LOESS curve. The two fitting lines were similar across most of the age range, so we included baseline age as a linear term. We therefore used generalized estimating equations (GEE) because our main goal was to compare how average memory scores changed over time in the memory training and control groups. GEE allowed us to estimate these group-level changes while accounting for the correlation between repeated scores from the same participant.


## Results

Tables, graphics, and statistics, Oh my!

Talk about the results, but don't tie it to your main question/topic (yet!).

```{r results = "hide", echo = FALSE}
#echo = FALSE forces it to not show the code
#results = "hide" hides the output but shows the code
memory_data %>%
  filter(Years == 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = AgeAtBaseline, y = Memory)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "blue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Memory Scores At Baseline Age",
    x = "Baseline Age",
    y = "Baseline Memory Score"
  ) +
  theme_classic()

memory_data %>%
  mutate(Pred = predict(gee_mod2),
         Resid = Memory - Pred
         ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Pred, y = Resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, color = "purple") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "Memory Training Model Residuals",
    x = "Predicted Memory Score",
    y = "Residual"
  ) +
  theme_classic()

booster_data %>%
  mutate(Pred = predict(gee_booster),
         Resid = Memory - Pred
         ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Pred, y = Resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, color = "purple") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "Booster Training Model Residuals",
    x = "Predicted Memory Score",
    y = "Residual"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```
